topics: 🕊️ Entering the Covenant Without a Temple — Rebbi's threefold requirement for converts, and how conversion continues without sacrifices
⚖️ Four Who Bring an Offering for Intentional as for Unwitting Sin — the maidservant, the impure nazirite, and two false oaths
👩‍👩‍👧 Five Maidservants vs. One, Five Times — Rabbi Yoḥanan's rule on separate bodies versus repeated lapses
🔄 Five Who Bring One Offering for Many Transgressions — how repetition collapses multiple sins into a single offering
🤰 Multiple Births, One Offering — the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda dispute which fetus 'causes' the woman's obligation

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Converts, Repeated Sins, and Multiple Births
overview.subtitle: Keritot 9a–9b
overview.hebrewSource: חֲמִשָּׁה מְבִיאִין קׇרְבָּן אֶחָד עַל עֲבֵירוֹת הַרְבֵּה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf finishes analyzing the convert's atonement offering — modeled, per Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, on how the Jewish people themselves entered the covenant at Sinai through circumcision, immersion, and the sprinkling of blood — and explains how conversion continues even without a Temple. A new mishna then lists four transgressors who bring the very same offering whether they sinned intentionally or unwittingly (the espoused maidservant's partner, the impure nazirite, and two false oaths), followed by a mishna listing five people who bring only a single offering no matter how many times they repeated the same transgression. The daf closes with a mishna on a woman who gives birth or miscarries repeatedly in overlapping periods of purification, where the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda dispute exactly which pregnancy anchors her single obligatory offering.

slides.title: 🕊️ Entering the Covenant Without a Temple
slides.subtitle: Rebbi models the convert's rite on Israel's own entry into the covenant at Sinai

nodes.content: 📜 Rebbi: 'As you are, so shall the stranger be' (Num. 15:15) means as your ancestors were — entry required circumcision, immersion, and sprinkled blood
❓ Objection: if all three are required by Torah law, how can converts be accepted today, when there is no Temple for the blood-offering?
✅ Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov: the verse itself says 'throughout your generations' — converts are accepted in every era, offering or not
💰 Practical follow-up: a baraita required a convert today to set aside a quarter-dinar for a future offering
🚫 Rabbi Shimon: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai's court already nullified this practice, fearing accidental misuse of the set-aside money

callout.label: Ruling:
callout.text: The halakha follows Rabbi Shimon — no money need be set aside.

slides.title: ⚖️ Four Who Bring an Offering for Intentional as for Unwitting Sin
slides.subtitle: A new mishna: these four owe the identical offering regardless of intent
rows: One who has relations with an espoused maidservant
'For his sin that he has sinned' (Lev. 19:22) — the doubled phrase equates unwitting and intentional
The word 'suddenly' (פִּתְאוֹם) can mean intentional or beyond-control; paired with 'unexpectedly' (פֶּתַע, unwitting) to show the offering covers all three
One who falsely swears the oath of testimony
Unlike other sliding-scale cases, the Torah omits 'and it be hidden from him' — showing intent doesn't change liability
One who falsely swears the oath on a deposit
Derived by verbal analogy ('shall sin' / 'shall sin') from the oath of testimony

callout.label: Why these four?
callout.text: In every other case, only an unwitting sin brings a sin offering; intentional sin brings a harsher penalty instead. These four are exceptions where the same offering covers both.

slides.title: 👩‍👩‍👧 Five Maidservants vs. One, Five Times
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Ḥanina of Tirna'a questions Rabbi Yoḥanan on separate bodies

lines.speaker: R' Ḥanina
lines.text: If one has relations with five different espoused maidservants in a single lapse of awareness, is he liable for one offering or five?

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan
lines.text: Liable for each and every one — five separate offerings.

lines.speaker: R' Ḥanina
lines.text: But the mishna says multiple acts with one maidservant require only one offering — what's the difference?

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan
lines.text: One maidservant means the acts share a single body (גּוּפָא); five maidservants means five separate bodies — and separate bodies always divide liability.

lines.speaker: R' Ḥanina
lines.text: Where is 'separate bodies divide liability' derived for a maidservant specifically?

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan
lines.text: Just as forbidden relations divide by 'a woman' (Lev. 18:19), the maidservant verse (Lev. 19:20) likewise says 'a woman, and she is a maidservant' — dividing liability by each woman.

callout.label: Principle:
callout.text: Repetition with the same body collapses into one offering; the same act with different people never does.

slides.title: 🔄 Five Who Bring One Offering for Many Transgressions
slides.subtitle: A mishna: repeated violations of the same prohibition, by the same person against the same target, still cost only one offering

boxes.title: Repeated acts, one body
items: Many acts of intercourse with the same espoused maidservant
A nazirite impure many times — but only works per Rabbi Yosei b. Rabbi Yehuda's view that purity-naziriteship starts on day 7, so repeated 7th-day impurity never reaches the offering-eligible 8th day

boxes.title: Repeated warnings / afflictions, one legal event
items: A husband's jealousy warnings against several men — 'law of jealousies' (plural) teaches one law for many warnings
A leper afflicted with leprosy multiple times before completing purification — 'this is the law of the leper' covers all relapses

callout.label: The fifth case:
callout.text: A woman who gives birth to multiple offspring — introduced by the next mishna, and the subject of the daf's final debate.

slides.title: 🤰 Multiple Births, One Offering — Which Birth 'Causes' It?
slides.subtitle: A woman who miscarries repeatedly within overlapping 80-day purification periods

lines.speaker: Case
lines.text: A woman miscarries a female fetus, then miscarries again within that fetus's 80-day purification period, then miscarries a third time within the second period.

lines.speaker: The Rabbis
lines.text: She brings one offering total ('this is the law of the woman who bears,' Lev. 12:7) — and she counts her purification period from the second (most recent) fetus.

lines.speaker: Rabbi Yehuda
lines.text: She brings an offering for the first miscarriage, none for the second (absorbed into the first's period), then a separate offering for the third (since it fell after the first period ended).

lines.speaker: Extended even to twins
lines.text: The Gemara stresses Rabbi Yehuda's position applies even to a woman miscarrying twins from a single pregnancy — one might have thought he'd concede there, but he does not.

callout.label: Underlying question:
callout.text: Does the obligation 'reset' with each new pregnancy event (Rabbis: the most recent triggers it) or 'anchor' to the first (Rabbi Yehuda: the earliest triggers it, with later ones assessed against its own clock)?

summary.principle: Multiple violations collapse into a single offering only when they share the same legal 'body' or event — a single maidservant, a single naziriteship, a single set of warnings, or overlapping purification periods — but separate bodies, like five different maidservants, always require separate offerings.

flowSteps.content: 🕊️ Converts enter the covenant through circumcision, immersion, and blood — but Temple absence never bars conversion
⚖️ Four transgressors (maidservant, impure nazirite, two false oaths) owe the same offering whether intentional or unwitting
👩‍👩‍👧 Five separate maidservants require five offerings; five acts with one maidservant require only one

columns.content: 🔄 Repetition against the same target (maidservant, nazirite's purity term, jealousy warnings, leprosy) yields one offering
🤰 Overlapping births/miscarriages: Rabbis anchor to the latest fetus, Rabbi Yehuda to the earliest

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: whether one offering or many are owed always turns on whether the repeated acts share one 'body' or event, or constitute genuinely separate ones

quiz.q: According to Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov, how can converts be accepted today, when there is no Temple to bring the atonement offering that Rebbi says is required for entering the covenant?
o: Converts cannot be accepted today at all
The verse 'throughout your generations' teaches that converts are accepted in every era, even without an offering
A substitute animal is always available
Only the immersion is truly required
quiz.e: Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov derives from 'throughout your generations' (Numbers 15:14) that the acceptance of converts continues across all eras, regardless of whether the Temple offering can currently be brought.

quiz.q: According to the mishna, which of the following is NOT one of the four who bring an offering for an intentional transgression the same as for an unwitting one?
o: One who has relations with an espoused maidservant
A nazirite who became ritually impure
One who eats forbidden fat
One who falsely swears the oath of testimony
quiz.e: Eating forbidden fat is not among these four; ordinarily, an unwitting sin brings a sin offering while an intentional one brings a harsher penalty. The four exceptions are the maidservant case, the impure nazirite, and the two false oaths (testimony and deposit).

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yoḥanan, why is one liable to bring five separate offerings for having relations with five different espoused maidservants in one lapse of awareness, while multiple acts with a single maidservant require only one offering?
o: Because five maidservants is always a capital case
Because five separate maidservants constitute separate 'bodies,' each requiring its own offering, unlike repeated acts with one body
Because the Torah specifically counts to five
Because maidservants are treated like forbidden animals
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan explains that liability divides according to separate bodies (individuals); repeated acts with the same maidservant share one body and thus one offering, while five different maidservants are five separate bodies requiring five offerings.

quiz.q: Whose opinion does Rav Ḥisda say the mishna (that a nazirite impure multiple times brings only one offering) must follow, and why?
o: Rabbi Meir, because he is lenient generally
Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, because he holds the naziriteship of purity begins on the seventh day, so repeated seventh-day impurities never reach an offering-eligible moment
Rabbi Akiva, because he requires no action for liability
Rabbi Shimon, because of his general leniency toward nazirites
quiz.e: Rav Ḥisda explains that only according to Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda (naziriteship of purity begins on day seven), can repeated seventh-day impurities combine into one offering; according to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the case wouldn't work this way.

quiz.q: In the case of a woman who miscarries three times within overlapping 80-day purification periods, how does Rabbi Yehuda's view differ from the Rabbis' view?
o: Rabbi Yehuda says she brings no offering at all

The Rabbis anchor her single offering to the most recent (second) fetus; Rabbi Yehuda brings an offering for the first miscarriage and a separate one for the third, which fell outside the first's purification period
Rabbi Yehuda requires a separate offering for every single miscarriage
There is no actual disagreement between them
quiz.e: The Rabbis hold that the woman's purification period counts from the second (most recent) fetus, requiring one offering total; Rabbi Yehuda holds the first fetus anchors the period, so the second is absorbed into it, but the third — falling after that period ends — requires its own separate offering.
